Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
ARGUMENT

**DEFENDANT'S LETTER VIOLATES THE FDCPA IF THE LEAST SOPHISTICATED DEBTOR COULD REASONABLY READ IT TO HAVE TWO OR MORE MEANINGS, ONE OF WHICH IS INACCURATE.**

**A. The Act is read broadly and from the vantage of the least sophisticated debtor.**

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) prohibits any "false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt," 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, including "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt," *id.* § 1692e(10). Because the Act is remedial, this Court construes its language broadly to effect its purpose. *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006).

Whether a letter is deceptive is judged from the perspective of the least sophisticated debtor. *Id.* at 453–54; *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008). That standard is lower than that of the reasonable debtor. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454. It ensures that the Act protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000) (citation omitted). The inquiry is objective. It asks what the letter could convey to the least sophisticated recipient, not what a careful or experienced reader would understand.

**B. A letter open to a reasonable but inaccurate reading is deceptive.**

From that standard follows a settled rule: a collection letter "is deceptive when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455 (quoting *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354). A collector therefore cannot escape liability merely because one available reading is true. The violation lies in exposing the debtor to a reasonable, false understanding.

This Court has applied these protective principles to varied forms of misleading communication. In *Brown*, a letter warned that a failure to cooperate "could" result in legal action. The Court reversed dismissal because the least sophisticated debtor could be deceived if such action was not in fact intended or likely. 464 F.3d at 455. Conditional phrasing did not immunize the letter. In *Rosenau*, a letter from the collector's "Legal Department" could be read to come from an attorney, so judgment on the pleadings for the collector was improper. 539 F.3d at 223–24. In *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 1003 (3d Cir. 2011), letters on law-firm letterhead were deceptive because they could lead the least sophisticated debtor to believe an attorney was involved in collecting the debt, notwithstanding a disclaimer. And in *Tatis v. Allied Interstate, LLC*, 882 F.3d 422, 427–30 (3d Cir. 2018), an offer to "settle" a time-barred debt stated a claim because the least sophisticated debtor could understand it to mean the debt was legally enforceable.

**C. The rule's limits do not shelter a reasonable misreading.**

The standard does not impose liability for "bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations," and it presumes "a basic level of understanding and willingness to read with care." *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55 (citation omitted). The letter must also be read in its entirety. *See Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 299 (3d Cir. 2008) (rejecting debtors' claim of deception). And a false statement is actionable under § 1692e only if material, meaning capable of influencing the least sophisticated debtor's decision. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 421 (3d Cir. 2015). These limits screen out strained readings and immaterial errors. The two-meanings rule, however, does not require that the inaccurate reading be the only one available. It is enough that the reading is reasonable and material.

Defendant's letter fails this test. It states: "[quote the challenged language]." The least sophisticated debtor, reading the whole letter with care, could reasonably take that language to mean [accurate meaning] or, instead, [inaccurate meaning]. The second reading is false because [facts]. It is material because it could influence whether, when, or how the debtor pays or disputes the debt. Nothing elsewhere in the letter dispels the confusion. [Address any language Defendant contends is clarifying.] The letter therefore violates 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, including § 1692e(10).
